judgments.text:
Serial No.02
Regular List
HIGH COURT OF MEGHALAYA
AT SHILLONG
Crl.A.No.9/2023 with
Crl.M.C.No.32/2023
Date of Order: 01.06.2023
Grenath Ch. Marak Vs. State of Meghalaya
Coram:
Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sanjib Banerjee, Chief Justice
Hon’ble Mr. Justice W. Diengdoh, Judge
Appearance:
For the Appellant : Mr. S.D. Upadhaya, Legal Aid Counsel with
Mrs. A. Synrem, Adv
For the Respondent : Mr. B. Bhattacharjee, AAG with
Mr. S. Sengupta, Addl.PP
Mr. J.N. Rynjah, GA
i) Whether approved for reporting in Yes
Law journals etc.:
ii) Whether approved for publication

JUDGMENT: (per the Hon’ble, the Chief Justice) (Oral)
This appeal has been carried some 10 years after the conviction
of the appellant.
2. Since it appeared that the appellant was from the economically
weaker section of society and not literate, sufficient latitude was shown in
condoning the delay in receiving the appeal. At any rate, when it is a
person’s liberty at stake, courts are bound to be lenient in condoning the
delay.
Page 1 of 13
3. The appellant has been convicted under Section 302 read with
Sections 376A and 201 of the Penal Code, 1860. The first ground that the
appellant urges is that Section 376A of the Penal Code could not have
been invoked in this case since such provision was introduced by an
amendment of 2013, whereas the incident complained of in the present
case was of July 10, 2010.
4. Since the appellant has been convicted, inter alia, under Section
302 of the Penal Code, even if Section 376A had been wrongly invoked,
it would not affect the matter since the anomaly can be corrected at this
stage.
5. The further ground raised on behalf of the appellant is that no
statement made has been recorded by the investigating officer
culminating in the appellant allegedly leading the investigating agency to
where the body of the minor girl was found. The final ground urged on
behalf of the appellant is that the trial court failed to explain the
testimonies of the prosecution witnesses to the appellant or elicit any
response from the appellant in such regard. The appellant says that in
course of the appellant’s examination under Section 313 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973, questions were put by the court to the
appellant whose answers have been self-incriminating.
Page 2 of 13
6. The first information report in this case was lodged by the
father of a 12-year-old girl on July 13, 2010 at the Garobadha
Investigating Centre, following which a case was recorded at Tura Police
Station. The FIR revealed that the father of the victim had left home on
July 10, 2010 and was followed thereafter by his wife who went to attend
the Jhum cultivation. When both the husband and wife returned late in the
evening, they found their 12-year-old daughter missing and made
enquiries that evening and the following day and discovered only the day
after that some persons had seen the missing girl accompanying the
appellant herein on July 10, 2010. The FIR also revealed that in their
attempt to find out the girl, the local villagers went to the appellant’s
native village at Gildinggre to enquire of him, “but on the way at Okapara
the villagers caught him and brought him to the village at Balalgre.” The
FIR proceeded to record that the appellant confessed that on July 10,
2010, he had taken the girl and raped her before killing her by
strangulation. The FIR also claimed that the appellant had asserted that he
took the dead body of the girl to a jungle and threw it after tying her
hands behind her back with a gamcha.
7. In course of the trial, several of the prosecution witnesses,
including PW-3, asserted that the appellant herein had confessed before
such witnesses and several other villagers as indicated in the FIR. Indeed,
Page 3 of 13
it also came out from the evidence that the appellant did not return home
on July 10, 2010, the day the victim went missing and the appellant’s wife
testified to such effect. The other important evidence adduced on behalf
of the prosecution was that in the presence of several of the witnesses
called by the prosecution, the appellant herein led the police to where the
body of the victim was thrown, whereupon the body was discovered and
sent for post-mortem examination. The medical report revealed that the
victim had been raped and was also subjected to unnatural sex.
8. It is not necessary to dwell elaborately on the rest of the
evidence, particularly since the other parts of the evidence may not have
been summarised and put to the appellant in course of his examination
under Section 313 of the Code by the trial court.
9. However, what is evident from the recording of such
examination under Section 313 of the Code is that the evidence of the
wife of the appellant to the effect that the appellant did not return home
on July, 10 or thereafter, was put to the appellant and the appellant,
initially claimed that he was not at home, but later suggested that his wife
may not have spoken the truth. The trial court pointedly referred to the
evidence of PW-3 to the effect that after three days of search for the
missing girl and the appellant by the villagers, the villagers were able to
Page 4 of 13
nab the appellant. The appellant’s response was: “It is a fact that I was
caught.”
10. The trial court further put it to the appellant that PW-3 had
testified that the appellant had confessed that he had killed the girl before
PW-3 and the villagers. The appellant denied that he made such a
confession. The trial court then proceeded to take out another piece of the
evidence from the testimony of PW-3 to ask the appellant whether the
appellant had promised to show the dead body of the girl to the villagers.
Before adverting to the appellant’s response to such question, it must be
recorded that PW-3 did testify that the appellant herein led the police and
the villagers to where the dead body could be found in the jungle.
11. The appellant confirmed to the trial judge that he showed where
the dead body was and that at such time the police had accompanied him.
12. Through another question from the trial court in connection
with the post-mortem report, the trial court sought to elicit information
from the appellant herein regarding the possible murder of the girl. The
appellant’s response to question No.13 put in such regard was as follows:
“The Post Mortem report is wrong and the girl died of injuries
caused by a boulder falling on her chest, when I was lifting the
boulder. This incident happened in the Jhum. I got scared and
threw the dead body in the jungle.”
13. The further information that the appellant herein proffered to
the trial court was that the girl had died at about 1:30 pm and the
Page 5 of 13
appellant threw the dead body in the jungle at about 7 pm. He also
claimed that after he was caught by the villagers at Okapara village, he
wanted to tell them about the circumstances in which the girl met her
death, but he could not do so because he was beaten up and apparently
tortured by the villagers.
14. To deal, first, with the anomaly in the judgment of conviction
dated July 4, 2013 and the consequent sentence pronounced on July 24,
2013, it must be recorded that no case under Section 376A of the Penal
Code could have been made out and the reference to such provision was
palpably erroneous on the part of the trial court since even the charge-
sheet which was forwarded to the court on July 14, 2010 did not refer to
Section 376A, but referred, instead, to Sections 376, 377, 302 and 201
IPC.
15. As to the basis for convicting the appellant herein, first there
was the assertion by several persons as to the appellant’s confession.
Next, there was the appellant’s categorical statement that he led the police
to the body of the victim. Finally, the appellant claimed that he was the
only person present with the victim at the time the victim met her death,
but made no attempt to establish how the victim met her death. In any
event, the medical report did not corroborate the appellant’s version that
the victim was hit by a large boulder and was killed thereby.
Page 6 of 13
16. If, indeed, a heavy boulder landing on the chest of the victim
had killed the victim, the post-mortem report would have revealed the
same. Further, not only did the post-mortem report completely discredit
the appellant’s version of how the victim met with her death, such
medical examination report found that the victim had been subjected to
sex and even unnatural sex. Since the victim was a minor, any sex with
the victim would have amounted to a statutory rape and the consequence
would be conviction under Section 376 of the Penal Code. Accordingly,
the conviction of the appellant under Section 376A of the Penal Code is
annulled and set aside and the conviction in such regard as indicated to be
under Section 376 of the Penal Code.
17. The body of the victim in this case was found in a jungle, which
may be considered to be a remote, even though a somewhat accessible
place. When a person who was last seen with the would-be victim leads
the police or other persons to a place from where the body of the victim is
discovered, it is incumbent on such person to indicate the circumstances
in which he came to know of the location of the body and unless a
credible explanation is proffered, an adverse inference may be drawn
against him.
18. Further, when the appellant herein admitted that he was alone
with the victim when the victim met her death, it was incumbent on the
Page 7 of 13
appellant to prove how the victim came to meet her death. In such regard,
the appellant has failed miserably since the appellant’s assertion that a
large boulder fell on the chest of the victim and killed her is belied by the
post-mortem examination conducted on the body of the victim. To boot,
the medical report referred to the victim having been raped and subjected
to unnatural sex. In the circumstances and the evidence that was presented
before the trial court, it was perfectly in order for the trial court to arrive
at a conclusion that the appellant, in the absence of a satisfactory
explanation, must have committed the offence. It is also the fairly
admitted position that the appellant attempted to conceal the evidence by
throwing away the dead body. As a consequence, there does not appear to
be any reason to interfere with the impugned judgment of conviction or
the consequent sentence.
19. It may be recorded in this context that Section 313 of the Code
of 1973 casts an obligation on the trial judge to examine the accused and
explain and indicate to the accused any circumstances appearing in the
evidence against him. However, notwithstanding such duty, the provision
empowers the court, at any stage and without any previous warning, to
put questions to the accused that the court considers necessary. Indeed, at
the time that the summary of the evidence against the accused is presented
Page 8 of 13
by the trial court to the accused, the trial court is also authorised to
question the accused “generally on the case.”
20. Thus, the trial court is not a kind of a tape-recorder at the end of
the trial to merely summarise the evidence adduced against the accused
by the prosecution and seek the response of the accused thereto. Both, at
any stage of the trial and at such stage of examination under Section 313
of the Code, it is open to the court to put questions to the accused to
ascertain the circumstances pertaining to the case.
21. It must also be acknowledged, in the same breath, that when
there is some material which comes to light in course of the oral
testimonies of the prosecution witnesses and the same is not presented to
the accused in course of the accused being examined under Section 313 of
the Code, there is an element of prejudice that the accused may suffer.
This is more so when the accused may be unlettered and may not be able
to follow the drift of the evidence, despite being present in court.
22. It is for such reason that Section 313 of the Code has been
judicially interpreted to imply that all incriminating material against an
accused must be presented to the accused by the trial court for the accused
to be able to deal with the same and attempt to proffer a plausible
explanation therefor. But once the accused is presented with such
opportunity, if there is something which appears to be within the special
Page 9 of 13
knowledge of the accused, a mere denial of the material against the
accused would not suffice without the accused discharging his burden in
the circumstances, depending on the state of evidence.
23. In the present case, it was perfectly possible to construct a
judgment of conviction against the appellant herein based only on the
material put to him in course of his examination under Section 313 of the
Code and his response thereto. Indeed, as it appears from the impugned
judgment of July 4, 2013, much weightage was given by the trial court to
the effect that the appellant’s wife indicated that the appellant had also
gone missing from his home from July 10, 2010 and may not have
returned home till he was apprehended by the villagers at Okapara.
Doubtless, the state of mind of the appellant herein as revealed from his
immediate conduct, would have also weighed with the trial court. Here
was a man who was last seen with a minor victim and was not seen for the
next three days when the victim also remained untraced. He did not return
home or to his native village and was discovered somewhere else.
24. It is possible that the appellant’s conduct was completely
honourable and that the victim met an accidental death as described by the
appellant. It is equally understandable that the appellant may have been
scared and, as a reaction thereto, may have attempted to do away with the
body of the victim and lie underground for some time. However, the
Page 10 of 13
appellant ought to have been able to reconstruct the happenings or the
circumstances that led to the accidental death of the victim and any
evidence in such regard could have been looked into and verified.
25. On the contrary, since the post-mortem examination of the
victim proved that she had met an unnatural death after having been raped
and subjected to unnatural sex, it was for the appellant herein to
demonstrate how the injuries came to be suffered by the victim. In the
appellant’s abject failure to furnish any plausible explanation, coupled
with the indication of the guilty mind of the appellant as he lay low, the
element of guilt could be sufficiently inferred from the appellant’s
immediate conduct. Add to this, the fact that the appellant led the police
and others to the spot from where the body of the victim was discovered
and the appellant admitted to having done so, it was established beyond
reasonable doubt that it was the appellant who had committed the
offences of rape and murder of the victim.
26. Finally, even if some credence is to be given to the appellant’s
assertion that the victim met with an accidental death and the appellant
was so taken aback by the turn of events that he thought it best to throw
the body in the jungle and lie low, the one act of the appellant that is a
complete gave-away is the fact that the appellant tied the hands of the
victim behind her with a gamcha. Such an act would be more in tune with
Page 11 of 13
preventing a would-be victim from resisting strangulation. At any rate, the
fact that the girl’s hands were tied with a gamcha, which the appellant
apparently claimed to have done, would be completely inconsistent with
the scared reaction of a person whose companion meets with an
accidental death.
27. Further, irrespective of what the evidence was as to anyone
having noticed the girl accompanying the appellant, it was the appellant’s
admission that he was with the girl at the time that the girl met with her
death. Since the appellant had no explanation as to how the girl came to
be raped or subjected to unnatural sex and the appellant’s version of the
cause of death was belied by the medical report, there was no room for
any possible doubt that it was the appellant who had lured the girl and
committed rape on her before killing her and doing away with her body.
28. In such circumstances, the judgment of conviction of July 4,
2013 is modified by finding the appellant guilty under Sections 302 and
201 of the Penal Code together with Section 376 thereof, instead of
Section 376A as erroneously referred to by the trial court.
29. As a consequence of the error in the judgment of conviction and
upon Section 376A of the Penal Code being found inapplicable, the order
of the punishment is modified to life imprisonment under Section 302 of
the Code together with life imprisonment under Section 376 of the Penal
Page 12 of 13
Code, both sentences to run concurrently. The enhanced sentence of life
imprisonment implying till the rest of the natural life of the appellant
herein as passed in terms of Section 376A of the Penal Code stands set
aside.
30. Crl.A.No.9 of 2023 is otherwise dismissed as being completely
devoid of merits.
31. Crl.M.C.No.32 of 2023 is disposed of.
32. Let an authenticated copy of this judgment and order be
immediately made available to the appellant free of cost.
(W. Diengdoh) (Sanjib Banerjee)
Judge Chief Justice
Meghalaya
01.06.2023
“Lam DR-PS

judgments.case_name: AB/52/2023 of GURUCHARAN SINGH PUNIYA Vs STATE OF MEGHALAYA AND 2 OTHERS
judgments.text:
Serial No. 01
Supplementary List
HIGH COURT OF MEGHALAYA
AT SHILLONG
AB. No. 52 of 2023
Date of Decision: 10.10.2023
Shri. Gurucharan Singh Puniya Vs. State of Meghalaya & Ors.
Coram:
Hon’ble Mr. Justice W. Diengdoh, Judge
Appearance:
For the Petitioner/Appellant(s) : Mr. A.K. Bhuyan, Adv. with
Mr. J. Shylla, Adv.
For the Respondent(s) : Ms. N.G. Shylla, Sr. GA.
i) Whether approved for reporting in Yes/No
Law journals etc.:
ii) Whether approved for publication
in press: Yes/No
JUDGMENT (ORAL)
1. Heard Mr. A.K. Bhuyan, learned counsel for the petitioner as
well as Ms. N.G. Shylla, learned senior GA for the State respondents.
2. The learned counsel for the petitioner has submitted that by this
instant application, prayer for grant of transit bail for a period of 60(sixty)
days is prayed for, the fact being that the petitioner is a resident of Jowai in
1
the West Jaintia Hills District, Meghalaya and given the condition that he
is suffering from a number of ailments, for which he has also visited the
Jowai Civil Hospital and a report being obtained from the said hospital is
also annexed herein as Annexure-6. The said report would show that the
complaint of the petitioner is mainly connected with backache, in fact the
provisional diagnosis would show that his case is a case of chronic low
backache, for which according to the petitioner, he requires to go for
specialized treatment, particularly to New Delhi, but for the fact that he is
in pain, he could not do so at the relevant period.
3. The learned counsel also submits that the involvement of the
petitioner in connection with Sankrail P.S. Case No. 1144 of 2022 under
Section 419/420/467/468/469/471/408/120B IPC in the State of West
Bengal has also been referred in this connection, inasmuch as, in the said
Sankrail P.S. Case, cognizance was taken of an FIR filed by Jindal (India)
Limited against a number of persons and companies who are said to be
accused in the case and against whom investigation has been launched. It
also transpired that in course of investigation, the name of the petitioner
has figured, upon which the Investigating Officer has issued a notice under
Section 41-A Cr.P.C, calling upon the petitioner to appear before him at
Sankrail P.S. It is, at this stage, that the plea of the petitioner becomes
2
apparent since as stated above, the petitioner is not in a condition to appear
before the Investigating Officer because of the fact that he is required to
pursue his treatment at New Delhi immediately. Therefore, this application
for grant of transit bail is preferred before this Court.
4. The learned counsel for the petitioner has also submitted that it
is not the intention of the petitioner not to appear before the Investigating
Officer, but for an opportunity to be given to him to appear before the
Investigating Officer or the court of competent jurisdiction in the State of
West Bengal for necessary action from his part, on completion of his
medical treatment. It is only on this limited plea that this application is
filed before this Court and as such, the learned counsel prays that the
petitioner may be allowed to go on transit bail for a period of 60(six) days.
5. It is also the further submission of the learned counsel that
irrespective of the merits of the case, the petitioner would contest the same
at the appropriate time and forum, however, since there is an apprehension
of imminent arrest, therefore, this prayer is made herein.
6. The learned senior GA has strongly opposed the application,
firstly, on the ground that perhaps a notice under Section 41-A could not
have been issued by the concerned Investigating Officer since amongst the
alleged offences, the particular section of Section 467 IPC entails a
3
sentence of imprisonment for life or imprisonment for 10 years and fine,
the second objection raised by the learned senior GA is that, there is no
specific indication by the petitioner as regard his health condition and the
extent of his sickness or ailment, which would warrant this instant
application on such ground. Whatever document has been placed before
this Court in this connection, does not show that the petitioner is suffering
to the extent that he requires treatment outside the State and also that he
would not be able to appear before the Investigating Officer in response to
the said notice under Section 41-A. This application being without merits,
it may be dismissed is the further submission of the learned senior GA.
7. This Court having considered the submission made and also on
perusal of the application in hand, would agree with the learned counsel for
the petitioner that at this stage, the merits of the case, that is, the subject of
investigation may not be necessary to be gone into. The Court would only
consider the limited prayer made by the petitioner for grant of transit bail
as has been pointed out, and reference being made to a decision of this
Court in the case of Smti. Merry Bina Marak v. State of Meghalaya &
Anr, wherein vide order dated 31.10.2018 passed in AB. No. 22 of 2018,
this Court has dealt elaborately on the subject of transit bail and has come
to the conclusion that there is no bar for grant of the same. Para 19 of the
4
said order would be relevant, the same being reproduced herein below as:
“19. For the stated reasons and the law, I hold that
power to be exercised under Sections 438 and 482
CrPC rest with the High Court or Court of Sessions
within whose jurisdiction occurrence or part of
occurrence has taken place. However, for grant of
transitory pre-arrest bail regarding non-bailable
offences in the deserving cases, power of the High
Court or Court of Sessions within whose jurisdiction,
person resides or place where he apprehends arrest, is
permissible as such not barred. Therefore, accused can
invoke jurisdiction of the High Court or Court of
Sessions within whose jurisdiction he resides or place
where he apprehends arrest however, grant of pre-
arrest transit bail can’t be a matter of routine. Host of
circumstance, including heinousness of the crime have
to be taken care of.”
8. As observed above, though grant of pre-arrest transit bail
cannot be a matter of routine, the circumstances indicated by the petitioner,
that is, on ground of medical exigency, is found valid. The petitioner is
accordingly allowed to go on transit bail for a period of 60(sixty) days
from the date of this order. However, it is made clear that the petitioner
shall not abuse the liberty given, but would confine his activities only to
the extent of furtherance of his objective of getting proper medical
treatment from any place of treatment of his choice. It is also made clear
that at the end of the 60th day, he is directed to report before the
Investigating Officer of Sankrail Police Station, Detective Department,
5
Howrah Police Commissionarate, 24, Belilious Road, Kadam Tala,
Howrah, West Bengal-711101.
9. Needless to say, during this period of 60(sixty) days, the
petitioner shall not abscond or tamper with the evidence and witnesses
connected with the case and that he shall also bind himself on a personal
bond of ₹ 30,000/- (Rupees thirty thousand) only with one surety of like
amount to the satisfaction of the Arresting Officer.
10. In view of the above, this application is accordingly disposed
of. No costs.
Judge
Meghalaya
10.10.2023
“D. Nary, PS”

judgments.case_name: Crl.M.C./67/2022 of TARA MIAH Vs STATE OF MEGHALAYA
judgments.text:
Serial No.05
Regular List
HIGH COURT OF MEGHALAYA
AT SHILLONG
Crl.A.No.16/2022 with
Crl.M.C.No.67/2022
Date of Order: 11.07.2023
Tara Miah Vs. State of Meghalaya
Coram:
Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sanjib Banerjee, Chief Justice
Hon’ble Mr. Justice W. Diengdoh, Judge
Appearance:
For the Appellant : Mr. S.P. Mahanta, Legal Aid Counsel with
Mr. M. Lyngdoh, Adv
Mr. D. Dkhar, Adv
For the Respondent : Mr. N.D. Chullai, AAG with
Mr. A.H. Kharwanlang, Addl.Sr.GA
i ) W hether approved for reporting in Yes
Law journals etc.:
ii) Whether approved for publication
in press: Yes/No
JUDGMENT: (per the Hon’ble, the Chief Justice) (Oral)
This is quite an open and shut case except that considerable
time has been wasted on a wild goose chase that was eminently avoidable.
The distraction has to be dealt with before dealing with the merits of the
matter.
2. It appears that in the midst of the trial, the mother of the
appellant herein produced some prescriptions claiming to have been
issued by a psychiatrist who had treated the appellant. However, the trial
Page 1 of 11
judge recorded in his order of March 20, 2019 that the accused in the
dock did not show any sign of mental disorder as he interacted normally
and without any sign of mental disturbance.
3. The judge also went on to record that the medical test report of
the accused pertained to his liver functioning and though a psychiatrist’s
prescription of September, 2018 had been produced, the trial court
deemed it expedient that a specialist examine the appellant herein after
recording that the appellant’s mother claimed that since the appellant was
released on bail in 2018, the appellant seemed mentally disturbed and
“went roaming here and there hence, he was not found at home for which
he was rearrested.”
4. Accordingly, by the order of March 20, 2019, the trial court
directed the Superintendent of Tura jail to send the accused to a
psychiatrist in Tura hospital for check-up and examination of the mental
status of the accused and to submit a report in such regard by April 3,
2019.
5. The Superintendent of the District Jail, Tura complied with the
direction and had the appellant examined at Tura Civil Hospital. A report
in such regard was placed before the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Ampati
which was taken up by the court on March 29, 2019. The order passed by
the CJM on such date recorded exactly as follows:
Page 2 of 11
“Seen also the reason of referral filed by Smt. Chuontie Shira,
Clinical Psychologist, Tura Civil Hospital, wherein, it is
reported that the accused has no presence of cognitive
impairment and mental illness.
“It is also reported that he has the ability to reason out and
understand abstract concept including morality and that he has
also ability to analyses the consequence of action and lastly, it
is also reported that he has low impulse control. Seen also the
administration of Psychiatric evaluation...”
6. Accordingly, the matter was directed to be put up before the
Sessions Judge on April 3, 2019 as earlier directed by the Sessions Judge
in the order of March 20, 2019.
7. On April 3, 2019, the trial court took notice of the medical
report pertaining to the appellant herein as furnished by the clinical
psychologist in Tura Civil Hospital. Upon recording the findings of the
specialist, the trial court required the trial to proceed in right earnest. It is
evident that the specialist at the Tura Civil Hospital had found nothing
wrong with the appellant and the trial court duly accepted such report.
8. Following the evidence being recorded of the witnesses at the
trial, the appellant herein was examined under Section 313 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973. The evidence of each of the witnesses was
summarised and the key points therein brought out by the trial court for
the appellant to comment thereon. It is interesting to notice the appellant’s
response to the questions put to him by the trial court.
9. The trial court summarised the evidence of the FIR-maker, who
was the father-in-law of the victim and who claimed to have been an eye-
Page 3 of 11
witness to the incident. Upon the trial court seeking the appellant’s
response to the evidence adduced by PW-1, the appellant claimed that at
the time of the incident he was young and was apparently playing with the
deceased as the deceased was a friend of the appellant. He went on to add
that he saw five persons quarreling and they were his brother, mother, the
complainant, the complainant’s wife and the deceased. He asserted that
the victim was his nephew but even though he said that he was present at
the place of occurrence, he claimed that he was not aware as to who
assaulted the victim or stabbed the victim. He denied that he had assaulted
the victim and insisted that he had no quarrel with the victim as the victim
was his friend.
10. Interestingly, however, there appears to be a change of tack on
the part of the appellant in his response to the second question. Such
second question also pertained to the evidence of PW-1 and the assertion
by such witness that the appellant’s mother and brother were also present
at the place of occurrence. The appellant responded to such question by
asserting his innocence before claiming that the complainant dragged him
to the police station “because that time I was of unsound mind...” In
response to the subsequent questions, the appellant had little to say and
did not attempt to suggest his innocence, as he had done in response to the
first question, but maintained that he was mentally ill at the relevant point
Page 4 of 11
of time. Finally, upon the trial court enquiring of the appellant whether he
would call any witness, he clearly responded in the negative.
11. On a reading of the appellant’s examination and his response to
the questions put to him by the trial court after the witnesses had been
examined, it does not appear that the responses were incoherent or
unsound. After the initial attempt by the appellant to plead innocence, the
appellant resorted to plan B: that he was mentally unwell at the time of
the incident. However, the appellant admitted to have been present at the
place of occurrence and it is apparent that the appellant was a witness to
the incident and the appellant corroborated that at least the appellant’s
mother and brother along with the wife of the victim and the parents of
the victim were there or thereabouts at the place of occurrence.
12. It is elementary that for a person to be proceeded against for the
commission of a grievous offence as in the present case, the court must be
satisfied that he had committed the offence consciously and that he was fit
to stand trial for the commission of such act. Thus, an accused has to be
found both to have been in good mental capacity at the time of the
commission of the offence and in sufficiently good mental state to be able
to stand trial for his action.
13. No evidence was adduced on behalf of the appellant in support
of the somewhat irregular suggestion by the appellant’s mother at the
beginning of the trial that the appellant was of unsound mind. If the
Page 5 of 11
appellant was of unsound mind at the time of the commission of the
offence, it had to be demonstrated. No attempt in such regard was made
on behalf of the appellant. Following the trial court’s direction to have the
appellant clinically examined, the appellant was found to be in good
mental shape by the clinical psychologist attached to the Tura Civil
Hospital.
14. Quite needlessly, much is sought to be made by legal aid
Counsel of the fact that the trial court had required a psychiatrist to
examine the appellant but it was a clinical psychologist who had
conducted the examination. No attempt, however, is made to indicate that
a clinical psychologist cannot assess the mental condition or fitness of a
person. Indeed, it is a clinical psychologist who is the appropriate person
to assess the mental state or condition of a person. In any event, the report
furnished by the clinical psychologist indicated appropriate tests having
been conducted and, the trial court, upon due satisfaction in such regard,
proceeded with the trial.
15. Further, and more importantly, it is said that the judges’ eyes
and the judges’ assessment are probably the best and, in such regard, the
trial court recorded that the accused in the dock showed no signs of
mental imbalance or disorder and appeared to be perfectly oriented and
responsive.
Page 6 of 11
16. At the initial stage of the present appeal, since a ground of
mental instability or insanity of the convict was taken, this Court deemed
it proper to have the appellant examined. The appellant has been
examined both at the Meghalaya Institute of Mental Health and
Neurological Sciences and at the North Eastern Indira Gandhi Regional
Institute of Health and Medical Sciences and the reports clearly indicate
that the appellant is responsive, aware and conscious. The entire exercise,
including the charade by the appellant in course of his examination under
Section 313 of the Code was a diversion to scuttle the proceedings and
gain undue advantage by resorting to a needless trick.
17. There never was, nor is now, any merit in the assertion by or on
behalf of the appellant as to his mental capacity. No evidence was
adduced as to the appellant’s mental capacity at the time of the incident.
Both at the time of the trial and at the time of this appeal, the appellant’s
mental condition has been assessed by experts and the appellant was
found fit to stand trial and in perfect mental state as of now, at least for
the purpose of the present proceedings.
18. As to the merits, there appears to be very little to assess or
adjudicate. The first information report was lodged on September 17,
2010 by the father-in-law of the victim at the Monabari Police Station in
the West Garo Hills claiming that in course of a quarrel involving several
Page 7 of 11
persons, the appellant became ferocious and stabbed the victim with a
knife which caused the death of the victim.
19. In course of his deposition in court, the father-in-law of the
victim as PW-1 asserted that the incident took place at around 6:30 pm
when he was at home with his wife when the appellant came to the
witness’ house, started a quarrel with the victim and assaulted the victim
with a knife. In his cross-examination, the father-in-law of the victim
reiterated that he had witnessed the incident and it happened in the
presence of the mother and a brother of the appellant between 6 and 6:30
pm when it was not completely dark. For good measure, he repeated that
he saw the appellant striking the victim with a knife which the appellant
had drawn from his waist.
20. The wife of the victim was examined as PW-3. She claimed
that she was sitting in the verandah of the house when the appellant came
and started a quarrel with her deceased husband. According to the wife,
the quarrel pertained to a land dispute. The witness claimed that she saw
the accused with the knife stabbing the witness’ husband. In her cross-
examination, she repeated that she was present when the incident took
place just outside the victim’s house. She also claimed that the appellant’s
mother and a brother were present at the place of occurrence and repeated
that she had seen the appellant actually stabbing her husband with a knife.
Page 8 of 11
21. The mother of the victim was examined as PW-4. She claimed
that the incident took place right outside her house and she saw the
appellant assaulting the victim with a knife. However, in her cross-
examination, after saying that the appellant’s mother and an elder brother
were also present at the place of occurrence, she claimed that she was
inside the house and when she heard a scream, she claimed that she came
out and saw the victim lying on the ground and the appellant holding the
knife in his hand.
22. The investigating officer referred to a dagger measuring about
11½ inches which was the murder weapon. The relevant knife was
exhibited in court. According to the investigating officer, the complainant
and the complainant’s daughter were the eye-witnesses to the incident.
23. The doctor who conducted the post-mortem study was next
examined as PW-7 and he described the external injuries that would be
consistent with a person trying to ward off a knife brandished by a right
handed person. The medical examiner referred to the abdominal injuries
received by the victim and was of the opinion that the victim died due to
haemmorage of the abdominal organs and the shock following the assault.
Such medical practitioner indicated that he had conducted the post-
mortem examination at 3:15 pm on September 18, 2010 and his opinion at
the relevant point of time was that the victim had died of ante-mortem
Page 9 of 11
injuries inflicted on the victim some 24 to 26 hours prior to the post-
mortem examination.
24. On the basis of the evidence before the trial court, there was
little discussion which was necessary. The trial court reproduced the
material parts of the deposition of the witnesses and found that there was
nothing brought to detract from the eye-witnesses’ accounts and the
corroboration of the injuries and the cause of death by the post-mortem
examination.
25. By the judgment and order impugned dated February 12, 2020,
the trial court sentenced the appellant to life imprisonment upon
appreciating that for an offence committed under Section 302 of the Penal
Code, 1860 no lesser sentence than life imprisonment could be awarded,
if the maximum sentence of death penalty was found to be inappropriate.
Indeed, the manner in which the trial was conducted and the reasons
furnished in the judgment and order impugned are found to be
satisfactory. This was not one of the rarest of rare cases which would
warrant the capital punishment to be imposed.
26. Accordingly, Crl.A.No.16 of 2022 is dismissed by upholding
the judgment of conviction of February 12, 2020 and finding that an
appropriate punishment of rigorous imprisonment for life has been
awarded, together with a fine of Rs.5000/-. As indicated earlier, the minor
Page 10 of 11
distraction of the appellant being of unsound mind does not warrant much
attention particularly in the light of the expert opinions obtained recently.
27. Crl.M.C.No.67 of 2022 is disposed of.
28. Let an authenticated copy of this judgment and order be
immediately made available to the appellant free of cost.
(W. Diengdoh) (Sanjib Banerjee)

judgments.case_name: AB/3/2023 of MESHWA DKHAR Vs STATE OF MEGHALAYA
judgments.text:
Serial No. 10 & 11
Regular List
HIGH COURT OF MEGHALAYA
AT SHILLONG
A.B. No. 3 of 2023 with
A.B. No. 4 of 2023
Date of Decision: 07.03.2023
Shri Meshwa Dkhar Vs. State of Meghalaya
Shri Lowingstone Suchiang Vs. State of Meghalaya
Coram:
Hon’ble Mr. Justice W. Diengdoh, Judge
Appearance:
For the Petitioner/Appellant(s) : Mr. S. Thapa, Adv.
For the Respondent(s) : Mr. B. Bhattacharjee, AAG with
Mr. A.H. Kharwanlang, GA.
i) Whether approved for reporting in Yes/No
Law journals etc.:
ii) Whether approved for publication
in press: Yes/No
O R D E R
1. These two applications has been preferred under Section 438 Cr.PC
for grant of pre-arrest bail in connection with a single FIR dated 18.12.2022
for which a police case being Khliehriat PS Case No. 101(12)2022 under
Section 307/506/145/34 IPC r/w Section 21(1) of the Mines and Mineral
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, (MMDR Act) has been
registered. Accordingly, it is deemed expedient and convenient to take up
1
the same together and to pass a common order.
2. Heard Mr. S. Thapa, learned counsel for the petitioners who has
submitted that the facts of the case is that on 17.12.2022, at about 9:30-
10:00PM or so, the petitioners were driving their respective trucks
(Dumper) from Umtyra towards Khliehriat when some people tried to stop
their vehicles and since it was night time and the identity of the said persons
was not known to them, the petitioners did not stop for fear of their life and
property. However, the said persons chased the vehicles they were driving
and on realizing that a police vehicle was behind them, the petitioners
stopped their vehicles and was thereafter taken to Khliehriat Police Station.
At that point of time, a group of unknown people gathered at the police
station and used abusing language at the police and apprehending that the
situation may turn ugly, the petitioners fearing for their lives fled from the
scene. They later came to know that the police had registered an FIR against
them numbered as aforementioned.
3. Apprehending arrest, the petitioners has approached the Court of the
Sessions Judge/Special Judge, Khliehriat who is dealing with cases under
the MMDR Act for grant of anticipatory bail but the same was rejected vide
order dated 16.01.2023.
4. The learned counsel has submitted that even looking into the
provisions of the alleged offence said to have been committed by the
petitioners, the offence under Section 307 IPC cannot be sustained as there
is no prima facie evidence to indicate any intended attempt to murder by the
petitioners in the whole episode. The other sections are either bailable or
minor offences for which bail can be granted.
2
5. The petitioners being the sole bread earner of their family and having
no criminal antecedent, if arrested, their reputation and image in the society
will be tarnished for no fault of theirs.
6. It is therefore prayed that this petition may be allowed and that the
interim bail granted to the petitioners may be made absolute with any
conditions that this Court may deem fit to impose.
7. Per contra, Mr. B. Bhattacharjee, learned AAG has submitted that
the case diary as called for by this Court is produced before the Court today
and the same is submitted for perusal of the same.
8. Refuting the submissions made by the learned counsel for the
petitioner, the learned AAG has submitted that the case is very serious in
nature and the fact that the petitioners have been identified as the drivers of
the three trucks involved in the incident as stated by the petitioners wherein,
on being asked to stop by the police who were on NAKA duty did not do
so but instead rammed their vehicle at the police party with the intention to
kill them and also to escape checking would only goes to show that there is
no intention by the petitioners to cooperate with the law enforcing agency.
9. The next part of the incident is when a number of persons who had
come to the police station apparently to express support to the petitioners,
to the extent that abuses were hurled at the police personnel and in the
melee, the petitioners making good their escape would also prove that the
petitioners has a guilty conscience.
10. The learned AAG has also submitted that from the case diary, it can
be determined that the action of the petitioners does not exhibit a person
3
who is innocent and the offence being grave, at this stage pre-arrest bail
may not be granted and the interim bail granted may be discharged.
11. This Court have given considerable thought to the submission and
contention of the parties and have also perused the petition in hand as well
as the case diary.
12. Facts as stated above would indicate that the petitioners are accused
of not complying with the orders and directions of the law enforcing agency,
who while on NAKA duty had directed that petitioners to stop their vehicle,
presumably for checking, but the petitioners disregarded the said direction
and inspite of some persons being in front of their vehicle, did not stop but
proceeded forward, which in all probability could result in a fatal accident.
However, this Court will not come to any conclusion at this stage without
the evidence being fully collected. A perusal of the case diary would show
that there is prima facie evidence that the petitioners are involved in the
police case registered against them.
13. The first part of the provision of Section 438 Cr.PC provides that a
person who has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of
having committed a non-bailable offence, may apply to the High Court or
the court of Sessions with a prayer to be released on bail and the court may
allow such prayer after taking into consideration the following factors:-
(i) the nature and gravity of the accusation;
(ii) the antecedents of the applicant including the fact as to
whether he has previously undergone imprisonment on
conviction by a Court in respect of any cognizable offence;
4
(iii) the possibility of the applicant to flee from justice; and.
(iv) where the accusation has been made with the object of
injuring or humiliating the applicant by having him so
arrested, either reject the application forthwith or issue an
interim order for the grant of anticipatory bail…
14. In the case of Prasanta Kumar Sarkar v. Ashis Chatterjee and
Anr.: (2010) 14 SCC 496 at para 9, the Hon’ble Supreme Court has
reiterated the general principle of grant of bail when it has opined that while
exercising the power for grant of bail, the court has to keep in mind certain
circumstances and factors. The said para is reproduced herein below as:-
“9.... among other circumstances, the factors which are to be borne in mind
while considering an application for bail are:
(i) whether there is any prima facie or reasonable ground to be believed
that the accused had committed the offence.
(ii) nature and gravity of the accusation;
(iii) severity of the punishment in the event of conviction;
(iv) danger of the accused absconding or fleeing, if released on bail;
(v) character, behaviour, means, position and standing of the accused;
(vi) likelihood of the offence being repeated;
(vii) reasonable apprehension of the witnesses being influenced; and
(viii) danger, of course, of justice being thwarted by grant of bail.
15. The main consideration as far as grant of pre-arrest or anticipatory
bail is concerned is that, the applicant has to show that he or she apprehends
arrest for which the court can exercise this power. In this case, as pointed
out, the registration of the police case was in the month of December 2022,
the petitioners had preferred an application for grant of pre-arrest bail in the
5
month of January 2023 relatable to the order dated 16.01.2023 passed by
the learned Sessions Judge/ADC (J) Khliehriat, East Jaintia Hills rejecting
the application. Since the month of January 2023, the petitioners has
approached this Court only in the month of March 2023. This would give
the impression that there is no apprehension as such which would warrant
an immediate approach before this Court.
16. Be that as it may, the fact that the offence alleged is grave and serious
in nature, this Court relying on the principles aforementioned, is not
inclined to allow the prayer of the petitioners at this juncture.
17. Petition is accordingly rejected and dismissed.
18. The interim bail granted is hereby discharged.
19. Registry to send back the case diary.
Judge
Meghalaya
07.03.2023
“ N. Swer, Stenographer”

State of Meghalaya Vs. Abal M. Sangma

Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sanjib Banerjee, Chief Justice
Hon’ble Mr. Justice H. S. Thangkhiew, Judge

Page 1 of 11
JUDGMENT: (per the Hon’ble, the Chief Justice) (Oral)
In MC (WA) No.12 of 2023, the applicant seeks leave to appeal
against a judgment and order of May 2, 2023 passed in WP (C) No.83
of 2015 to which the applicant herein was not a party.
2. The applicant claims to be seriously prejudiced by the relevant
order to the extent that such order has directed a fresh investigation to
be conducted into an incident of 2015 at the behest of the father of a
person who was killed in what, according to the State and the applicant,
was an encounter between the State police and Garo National Liberation
Army insurgents.
3. WA No.13 of 2023 is the State’s appeal against the same order.
4. Since there is already an appeal that has to be looked into,
notwithstanding the fact that the order directing an investigation may
not be seriously prejudicial to the applicant in MC (WA) No.12 of 2023,
leave is given to such applicant to prefer the appeal as a person
aggrieved.
5. The appeals are taken up for immediate consideration.
6. According to both the appellants, particularly the State, pursuant
to information received by the police personnel in Tura, they took steps
to deal with a situation where suspected militants with new recruits
were apparently in hiding in Romba Adinggre. The police personnel
Page 2 of 11
took appropriate steps to gather adequate men and fire-power to reach
the spot and at about 5 am on March 4, 2015, they identified a country-
style hut to be where the militants had gathered.
7. The State submits that after the hut was surrounded, warnings
were issued to the occupants to come out without arms but such
warnings fell on deaf ears. According to the State, three persons
suddenly broke open the bamboo door of the hut and rushed out firing at
the police personnel. It was in such circumstances that the State claims
that the police had no option but to open fire and one of the militants
who was in the most advanced position sustained bullet injuries as a
result of the police firing and died immediately. The State’s version also
speaks of two others who had rushed out together with the deceased, but
there does not appear to be any trace of such persons.
8. Apart from the criminal cases instituted by the police authorities
pertaining to the incident, the father of the deceased lodged a complaint
to the effect that it was a fake encounter in which his son had been
gunned down mercilessly by the police. Pursuant to the investigation of
such case, nothing untoward was discovered and a final report was
submitted under Section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
Aggrieved by the investigation into the allegations levelled by him, the
Page 3 of 11
father of the deceased then instituted WP (C) No.83 of 2015 in this
Court. An interim order was passed on June 28, 2017 on such petition,
the operative part whereof is found at paragraph 4 of such order:
“4. In such circumstances, I am of the considered view that there
is only one way out and that is further enquiry by a Judicial
Officer from the judicial side. Accordingly, learned District
Judge, Tura is entrusted with the job to conduct a thorough
enquiry and to submit the report before this Court within 5(five)
months.”
9. It appears that the District and Sessions Judge, Tura conducted
an inquiry and filed a report running into some 25 pages and appended
photographs of the place of occurrence along with markings thereon.
10. The conclusion drawn by the relevant District and Sessions
Judge appears from the following passage towards the end of the final
paragraph of the report:
“36. ...It can be seen that the source information about GNLA
militants taking shelter was most probably a correct information
as the deceased was found trying to escaped by running away
and shooting with his gun at the same time and the subsequent
recovery of the Demand Note in his pocket and also the
recovery of 2 (two) Blank Demand Notes as well as the
detonator from his Bachelor’s Dormatory. However the
presence of two other persons with the deceased who are said to
have escaped could not be established.”
11. Such report of the relevant District and Sessions Judge was
considered in great detail by the writ court in course of the final hearing
of the petition. It is evident that the State opposed the prayer for an
Page 4 of 11
inquiry by the Central Bureau of Investigation on the ground that the
Criminal Investigation Department of the State had investigated into the
matter and even a further independent inquiry by the District and
Sessions Judge, Tura revealed that it was a genuine encounter based on
accurate information.
12. However, what weighed with the writ court appears from
paragraphs 46 to 48 of the impugned judgment and order dated May 2,
2023:
“46. This Magistrate, being EW27, Labenn Ch. Marak, who is
also the Block Development Officer (BDO), Rongram reached
the PO at about 10:00 to 11:00 am on the same day and along
with I/C Bamon and other police personnel entered the house,
the door which is made of bamboo was not broken and inside
the room, some bottles of foreign liquor was found as well as
some papers and part of a detonator were also found. This
witness has also noted that at the spot where the deceased son of
the petitioner was found lying face down, there was a slope
below the house of the deceased and indications of a person who
might have tumbled or skidded through the slope, such skid
mark or slip mark showing signs of only a single person running
towards the place where the deceased was lying. When he
checked the body, he found many entry wounds as well as
gracing bullet wound on the body of the deceased, the maximum
target and wounds on the body being at the back and buttock
area. This witness also saw one old pistol which appears to be a
country-made pistol with a jammed magazine just about a few
meters from the body of the deceased. I/C Bamon picked up the
pistol from the shallow water of a nearby stream and checked it
in front of him. He tried to take out the magazine, but could not
do it, as it was very hard to take it out and he has to use stone to
remove the magazine. There were two bullets in the magazine
and the pistol seems rusted.
Page 5 of 11
“47. While appreciating the evidence of the witnesses and also
the Forensic Science Laboratory Report, the learned District and
Sessions Judge has relied on the said FSL Report that the
country made pistol is found serviceable and the gun powder
residue which was detected in the liquid in a plastic container is
the handwash of the deceased and also gun powder residue
detected in two cotton swabs found at the residence of the
deceased to come to the conclusion that the deceased had fired
from the said gun which was seized. The fact that the deceased
had also failed to surrender but had ran out shooting in the
direction of the police in a bid to escape, upon which the police
has retaliated by firing upon him has also confirmed the
conclusion of the learned Enquiry Officer that a genuine
encounter had taken place. There is however, an observation that
police should have exercised restraint once they have seen the
suspect have fallen, which only goes to show that it was
accepted that excessive use of force by the police had taken
place.
“48. On an analysis of the observations made above, what is
clear is that there are two versions of the sequence of events
which occurred on the said date, that is, on 04.03.2015, one, on
the part of the witnesses who are the residents of the village and
another from the police personnel who were also part of the
operation. Evidently, what is noticed is that proper investigation
to find out the actual truth have not been adequately dealt with
by the Investigating Officer, inasmuch as in the investigation
conducted by the CID into the two respective FIRs, one filed by
the Circle Inspector B.N. Marak and the other filed by the
petitioner herein, the Investigating Officer therein have filed his
final report indicating that there is no credible evidence to
proceed with the investigation, the findings thereto being
contrary to the prima facie evidence, even at this stage, when
there are present two viewpoints proffered by two sets of
witnesses as to what exactly happened at the place of occurrence
on the said day, the IO ought to have put in more diligent effort,
failure to do so would only invite an adverse inference and
rectification of such failure is therefore well within the scope of
the powers of this Court under Article 226.”
Page 6 of 11
13. Upon appreciating the evidence including the account of an
Executive Magistrate who arrived at the place of occurrence within
hours of the deceased being killed, the writ court was satisfied that there
were two versions of the same incident. Further, the Executive
Magistrate’s description of the defunct country-made pistol that was
discovered near the body of the deceased, who still lay on the ground
head down, and the completely contrary report of the Forensic Science
Laboratory in such regard, quite naturally raised a degree of suspicion,
to allay which an independent investigation appears to have been called
for.
14. Indeed, the writ court observed that notwithstanding the
evidence of the Executive Magistrate who was present at the place of
occurrence shortly after the shooting took place, the District and
Sessions Judge’s reliance on the FSL report without discrediting the
ocular evidence of the Executive Magistrate was somewhat irregular.
Indeed, even if such aspect has not been harped on in the order
impugned, the same is implicit from the discussion in the paragraphs
quoted above.
15. There was further material for the writ court to be prompted to
call for an independent investigation notwithstanding receipt of the
Page 7 of 11
report from the District and Sessions Judge, Tura. For a start, the
Executive Magistrate present at the spot immediately after the incident
reported that the bamboo door of the hut was not broken. Such an
observation goes against the fundamental premise of the State police
that the militants broke open the door and rushed at the police
personnel. Secondly, several of the bullet injuries found on the person
of the deceased were on his back and his buttocks. Even if it is accepted
that such injuries were suffered once he had fallen on the ground and
may have been as a result of the overenthusiasm of the police personnel
to ensure that the suspected militant was dead; there was enough
material for the writ court to conclude that it was an overkill or
excessive action. Most importantly, the police’s version hinges on three
persons rushing out and shooting at the police personnel. If the rest of
the police story is to be believed that they had surrounded the entire area
and issued warnings, there was little possibility of the two others to
escape.
16. The observations herein will not prejudice the further
investigation that has been directed but the only object of the present
exercise is to emphasise on the anomalies that weighed with the writ
court to observe that there were different versions of the same incident.
Page 8 of 11
17. At any rate, even if it is accepted for argument’s sake that it was
a genuine encounter and the State police acted reasonably and
rationally, there remains a slur on the conduct of the State police since,
at the end of the day, it may be said that the State police itself
investigated into an allegation of a fake encounter brought against it and
gave itself a clean chit. It would be so much better for the State police if
the investigation, as has been directed by the order impugned, is
conducted by an independent external agency and the State police is
given a clean chit by such agency.
18. As far as the individual who has been granted leave to prefer an
appeal is concerned, the order impugned does not prejudice such person
any more than it affects the State. If such person was a part of the police
team on the relevant date, the independent investigation by the Central
Bureau of Investigation will bring things to light and if no wrongdoing
was committed by such person, there is no need for any apprehension
on his part.
19. Considering the nature of the incident, the material that was
available before the writ court and the grounds that have been clearly
indicated for requiring a fresh investigation into the incident to be
Page 9 of 11
conducted by an independent agency, the judgment and order impugned
do no call for any interference.
20. A final ground is urged on behalf of the State to the effect that
the parameters laid down by the Supreme Court for a CBI investigation
despite the State opposing the same have not been met in the present
case.
21. The fact that the police’s version is that the action taken on the
relevant date was against extremists, the fact that the father of the victim
and the local villagers have a different account of the incident than
depicted by the police and the fact that serious anomalies were noticed
by the writ court from the account of an Executive Magistrate which
does not tally with the official version rendered by the police, were
good grounds for the writ court to require another agency to investigate
into matter. There is no need for the State to harbour any misgiving
since, if the police action was justified, the fresh investigation, whether
by CBI or by any other agency, would reveal the same.
22. Accordingly, both the appeals, WA No.29 of 2023 and WA
No.13 of 2023, are dismissed. It is made abundantly clear that none of
the observations in the judgment impugned or in this order will
prejudice the State or persuade the investigating agency in any manner
Page 10 of 11
whatsoever. The investigating agency is left free to conduct its own
investigation and the State and its allied agencies should cooperate in
the matter so that the investigation can be concluded as early as possible
and, preferably, within six months from date.
23. A copy of this order will immediately be forwarded to the office
of learned DSGI attached to this Court for the same to be forwarded to
the appropriate CBI personnel for necessary action.
24. MC (WA) No.12 of 2023 and MC (WA) No.32 of 2023 are
disposed of.
25. There will be no order as to costs.
(H. S. Thangkhiew) (Sanjib Banerjee)
Judge Chief Justice

judgments.text:
Serial No. 01
Supplementary List
HIGH COURT OF MEGHALAYA
AT SHILLONG

Coram:

Appearance:

JUDGMENT AND ORDER (ORAL)
1. Heard Mr. A. Bhattacharya, learned counsel for the accused
Jumma Khan, represented by the petitioner Mr. Pradip Sinha who has
submitted that this is an application under Section 439 Cr.P.C with a
prayer for grant of bail on behalf of the accused Jumma Khan who was
arrested by the police in connection with Umiam P.S. Case No. 04 (01) of
2023 under Section 307/326/34 IPC.
2. The learned counsel has referred to the FIR lodged before the
1
Officer-in-Charge, Umiam Police Station, Ri-Bhoi District by Mr.
Abhineet Srivastava on 26.01.2023 at about 10:15 pm, wherein the
complainant/informant has stated that on 21.01.2023 at about 7:30 pm, he
along with three friends had come to Orchid Umiam Lake to attend an
event called “Riders Mania 23” organized by the Royal Enfield Riders
Association of Meghalaya (RERAM). After the registration process is
over, the said informant went inside the camp and on reaching near the
stage area, they saw Mr. Jumma Khan and three other persons drinking
alcohol. Suddenly, upon seeing them, Jumma Khan and the others attacked
him with a big size wooden log on his head, but he defended himself by
raising his right hand as a result of which the blow hit his forearm. After
the incident, the informant and his friends met the organizers of the event
on 22.01.2023 and they were requested to leave the camp. Thereafter, the
informant went back to his home town to Silchar for medical treatment
where it was revealed that his forearm has been broken.
3. On the basis of the said FIR, the police accordingly registered the
said Umiam P.S. Case No. 04 (01) of 2023 on 26.01.2023 and in course of
investigation launched, three persons were arrested including Jumma Khan
and later on, another three persons suspected to be involved in the incident
were also arrested and are now in judicial custody.
4. It is also the submission of the learned counsel that the accused
2
Jumma Khan and his friends are members of a Motor Bike Club named,
“Silchar Thumpers Bullet Club”, and on coming to know of the said event
called BOBMC (Brotherhood of Bulleteers Motorcycling Consortium)
Rider Mania at Orchid Resort, Umiam organized by the Royal Enfield
Riders Association of Meghalaya (RERAM), they had accordingly
registered themselves and reached Umiam on 21.01.2023 at 4:30 pm and
went into the tent, coming out of the same only at 8:30 - 9:00 pm for food.
5. The accused/petitioner Jumma Khan has however acknowledged
that both he, his friends as well as the informant and his friends were
present at the BOBMC event where once upon a time, they were also
members of the Silchar Thumpers Bullet Club, but due to the anti-club
activities by some of them, they have now parted ways.
6. The learned counsel has however submitted that the allegation
made by the informant in the said FIR as well as the events which took
place thereafter would only go to show that the said allegation are all
concocted and the alleged incident is imaginary, inasmuch as, the FIR
records that the incident occurred at about 7:30 pm on that day i.e.
21.01.2023 whereas, the accused Jumma Khan had come out of his tent
only at 8:30 pm, he was therefore never at the scene of the crime, if at all it
happened.
7. The learned counsel has also submitted that the inclusion of
3
Section 307 IPC is only to allow the police to immediately arrest Jumma
Khan and others, when prima facie, it is noticed that the informant himself
has stated that after the alleged incident, he was seriously injured, but had
returned to Silchar. It could not be imagined as to how he managed to ride
back to Silchar which is about 299 Kms from Shillong on his bike.
8. The learned counsel has however submitted that investigation
and evidence in course of trial will proved the innocence of the accused,
however at this point of time, this application has been preferred seeking
grant of bail on the ground that the accused Jumma Khan is a sick person
and is also now under treatment at the Civil Hospital, Nongpoh with a
severe case of diabetes for which he has to take insulin four times a day,
which is not possible while still in judicial custody or even at the Nongpoh
Civil Hospital.
9. It is also the submission of the learned counsel that the accused
Jumma Khan has been in custody since 25.03.2023 when he was arrested
and considerable time have elapsed, for which it can be assumed that the
process and progress of investigation has reached a stage where the
statement of the relevant witnesses have been examined and all other
preliminary steps have been taken and therefore, keeping the accused in
further custody is no longer necessary.
10. Stressing on the fact that the accused Jumma Khan is an ailing
4
person, therefore, for his proper medical treatment, he may be allowed to
be enlarged on bail with any conditions as deemed fit to be imposed by this
Court, submits the learned counsel.
11. Mr. S. Sengupta, learned Addl. PP appearing on behalf of the
State respondent has submitted that the case diary as called for is produced
before this Court today and on perusal of the same, this Court may be
pleased to reject this application.
12. It is also the submission of the learned Addl. PP that at this stage,
the Investigating Officer requires more time to complete his investigation
and it would be too premature to release the accused on bail without giving
adequate opportunity for the I/O to come to a finding on the complicity of
the accused Jumma Khan and others so as to file the charge sheet.
13. This Court has given due consideration to the submission made,
the accused Jumma Khan had forwarded a plea of alibi, inasmuch as, he
has denied being a party to the alleged assault upon the informant and has
also questioned the manner in which the police have registered the case,
inter alia, under the offence of attempt to murder (Section 307 IPC), when
as pointed out events would show that the informant was never seriously
injured since he could managed to travel back to Silchar and to come again
to Umiam Police Station to file his FIR after six days of the alleged
incident which would only cast doubts on the veracity of the allegation
5
made.
14. As submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner, it is
indeed a matter of evidence as to what actually happened on the said date
of incident, but it cannot be denied that the alleged incident of assault had
taken place in a public place with many people present. The informant had
also named some eye witnesses who in their statement before the police
had corroborated the narration of the informant.
15. This Court cannot venture to come to any conclusion on this
account as to whether the informant was indeed seriously injured as a
result of the alleged assault upon him or that the accused Jumma Khan and
others are the perpetrators of such an act. Prima facie, it does appear that
the incident had actually happened and the informant was indeed injured,
but as to who is the culprit or what is the extent of injuries sustained is a
matter of evidence in course of trial.
16. Time and again, while a competent court is called upon to decide
on a bail application as the present case, the Court is guided by well settled
judicial pronouncements, particularly of the Apex Court which has, in a
catena of judgments laid down the guiding principles and parameters to be
considered for grant or refusal of bail. Suffice it to say that the cardinal
principle of „bail and not jail‟ would hold good even today.
17. What could be understood is that the common factor to be taken
6
into account while considering an application for bail is the nature and
gravity or seriousness of the offence alleged, the character of the evidence,
the possibility of the accused absconding or not cooperating with the
investigation and trial and also the fact that the accused, if enlarged on bail,
may tamper with the evidence and witnesses.
18. Keeping in mind the aforementioned factors to be considered,
this Court is also drawn to the observation of the Hon‟ble Supreme Court
in the case of Sanjay Chandra v. CBI: (2012) 1 SCC 40, wherein at para
21 of the same, it has been observed that:
“21. In bail application, generally, it has been laid down
from the earliest times that the object of bail is to secure the
appearance of the accused person at his trial by reasonable
amount of bail. The object of bail is neither punitive nor
preventative. Deprivation of liberty must be considered a
punishment, unless it is required to ensure that an accused
person will stand his trial when called upon. The courts owe
more than verbal respect to the principle that punishment
begins after conviction, and that every man is deemed to be
innocent until duly tried and duly found guilty.”
19. On an overall consideration of the facts and circumstances of the
case, this Court is of the view that the accused Jumma Khan may be
released on bail on certain conditions. The fact that the accused is also a
sick person would also be one of the determining factors for this Court to
consider the prayer for grant of bail.
20. Accordingly, the accused is directed to be released on bail on the
following conditions that:
7
i) He shall not abscond or tamper with the evidence and
witnesses;
ii) He shall appear before the Investigating Officer as and when
required;
iii) He shall not leave the jurisdiction of India without prior
permission of the I/O or the Court concerned and
iv) He shall furnish a personal bond of ₹ 30,000/- (Rupees thirty
thousand) only with two solvent sureties of like amount to
the satisfaction of the concerned court.
21. Registry is directed to return the case diary to the learned Addl.
PP immediately.
22. Bail application disposed of. No costs.
Judge
Meghalaya
20.04.2023
“D. Nary, PS”

JUDGMENT AND ORDER (ORAL)
1. The writ petitioner being aggrieved by the orders passed
by the respondent No. 2 and 3, whereby he has been dismissed from
service, is before this Court seeking directions for the respondents to
reconsider the quantum of punishment inflicted upon him.
Page 1 of 7
2. The brief facts of the case are that the petitioner had
entered into service in the Police Department in the year 1992 as
Assistant Sub- Inspector (ASI), and after being promoted to the post
of Un-Armed Branch Sub-Inspector (UBSI) had been serving in the
Department for 30 years, till his dismissal from service. Disciplinary
Proceedings had been drawn up against the petitioner on 23.08.2021
on 3 Articles of Charge which were; unauthorized absent from duties,
gross misconduct, violation of lawful direction from superiors, apart
from negligence and dereliction of duties, which were stated to be in
violation of Rules 3, 3A and 3B of the Meghalaya Civil Services
(Conduct) Rules, 2019. Thereafter, on conclusion of the said
proceedings, wherein the petitioner admitted to all the charges as
framed, he was dismissed from service. Though, an appeal had been
preferred, the dismissal order was upheld by the respondents.
3. Mr. C.C.T. Sangma, learned counsel for the petitioner does
not dispute that fact that the petitioner had pleaded guilty to all the
charges, nor does he question the Disciplinary Proceedings for lack of
opportunity to defend himself or otherwise. The prayer before this
Court, is only on the quantum of punishment that has been inflicted
upon the petitioner, which he contends that taking into account the
long years of service and the nature of infractions, the punishment of
Page 2 of 7
dismissal from service, is too harsh, and on this point deserves some
consideration from this Court.
4. The learned counsel also argued that, for being absent from
duties, the only punishment that could have been inflicted was to
deprive the petitioner from Pay and Allowances for the periods of
absence. He further contended that at the most, punishment of
compulsory retirement, could have been given as provided in FR-57
of the Meghalaya Fundamental & Subsidiary Rules, 1984, to ensure
sustenance. In support of his submissions, the learned counsel has
relied upon the following judgments:-
i) Bishwanath Prasad Singh vs. State of Bihar & Ors.
reported in (2001) 2 SCC 305
ii) Central Industrial Security Force & Ors. vs. Abrar Ali
reported in (2017) 4 SCC 507
iii) Brijesh Chandra Dwivedi vs. Sanya Sahayak & Ors.
reported in (2022) 4 SCC 189
5. The learned counsel concludes his submissions by
submitting that the Hon’ble Supreme Court, taking into account such
cases, had interfered and passed orders granting limited reliefs as has
been prayed by the writ petitioners in the cases as cited above. He
therefore prays to this extent, that this Court pass such orders for
reconsideration of the punishment that had been inflicted upon the
petitioner.
Page 3 of 7
6. Mr. B. Bhattacharjee, learned AAG assisted by Mr. A.H.
Kharwanlang, learned GA for the State respondents has drawn the
attention of this Court to the affidavit filed on behalf of the
respondents, and submits that the proceedings which had culminated
at the dismissal of the writ petitioner is not a one-off incident, but in
fact on 10 different occasions since the year 1999, the petitioner was
a habitual absentee, for which he had already been imposed 5 minor
punishments and 2 major punishments for his misconduct.
7. The learned AAG has also submitted that the petitioner
failed to discharge his duties as assigned, and whenever called upon,
refused to receive office orders and communications, and has kept 20
cases pending for investigation for a long time, without justifiable
reasons, which has jeopardized the entire legal process. He further
submits that Rule-7 of the Meghalaya Services (Discipline & Appeal)
Rules, 2011, has also provided for such punishment, and with there
being no irregularities in the proceedings and the charges found all
proved, the punishment as inflicted was commensurate with the
misconduct of the petitioner.
8. I have heard the learned counsel for the parties, considered
their submissions and also examined the materials on record.
Page 4 of 7
9. Though, the writ petitioner does not question the
proceedings, and has come only against the quantum of punishment,
it would be expedient, however, to look at the Statement of Articles of
Charge frames against him, which are reproduced hereinbelow:-
“ARTICLE-I
UBSI Jerang A Sangma is found unauthorised absent
from duty w.e.f. 9th August 2021 till date as reported by
OC Tura PS which has reference to Tura PS GDE No.
12 Dtd. 10/08/2021. Whereas, in the previous instance
UBSI Jerang Sangma was found unauthorized absent
from duty w.e.f. 15th July, 2021 to 17th July, 2021 as
reported by OC Tura PS. This has a reference of Tura
PS GDE No. 06 Dtd. 15/07/2021. Further, based on the
report submitted by OC Tura P vide WT No.
T/PS/WT/Vol. I/67 Dtd. 04/08/2021 UBSI Jerang A.
Sangma is found to be irregular and missing from the
PS on multiple instances. His misconduct prima facie,
is a violation of Rule 3 & 3B of the Meghalaya Civil
Services (Conduct) Rules, 2019.
ARTICLE-II
UBSI Jerang A. Sangma has kept various cases
pending of Tura PS viz. (i) C/No. 68(03)15 U/S 397 IPC
(ii) C/No. 121(05)15 U/S 188/506/34 IPC (iii) C/No.
124(05)15 U/S 384/507/511 IPC (iv) C/No. 141(06)15
U/S 507 IPC (v) C/No. 164(07)15 U/S 324/34 IPC (vi)
C/No. 169(07)15 U/S 365 IPC (vii) C/No. 210(08)15 U/S
323/354/392/34 IPC (viii) C/No. 87(07)19 U/S 323/506
IPC (ix) 170(12)20 U/S 379 IPC & (x) C/No. 172(12)20
U/S 457/380 IPC (xi) C/No. 77(04)2015 U/S 380 IPC
